stages.title: Disadvantages of specialisation: quality
stages.sub: See how the same division of labour that boosts output can quietly erode craftsmanship.

steps.q: A shoe-line worker only glues soles, all day, every day. Is their job varied, or the same task over and over?
steps.right: The same task over and over
steps.hint: Think about what dividing the job into small parts does to each worker's task.
steps.pre: Splitting production this way means each worker does

steps.q: After years of only gluing soles, could that worker easily sit down and make a whole shoe by hand, start to finish?
steps.right: No, they never practised the other skills
steps.wrong: Yes, just as easily as before
steps.hint: They only ever practised one small step, not the full craft.
steps.pre: So their range of skills has become

steps.q: A worker who repeats one small motion never sees the finished shoe. Would they spot and fix a flaw out of pride?
steps.right: Less likely, they never see the finished product
steps.wrong: Just as likely as a worker who makes the whole shoe
steps.hint: Pride in a finished product usually comes from making the whole thing, not one repeated motion.

steps.prompt: Drag and drop the 3 key terms in the order they build on each other.

steps.q: Output per hour on the line goes up, but customers start returning shoes with poorly glued soles. Has productivity risen without cost?
steps.right: No, quality has fallen even as output rose
steps.wrong: Yes, more shoes made is a pure gain
steps.hint: Compare the productivity gain with what is happening to the finished shoes.
